114.t: Learning to play by ear and Tom McIntosh teaching chords
114.s: He learned from records by ear; Tom McIntosh showed him chords on the Brook Benton tour bus.
114.ch: Learning and Moody's Mood for Love
114.q: Listening to records. I’d hear something and then try to play it like I thought maybe it sounded. And that’s how I did. And I played by ear for the longest time. And Tom McIntosh is the one that showed me changes you see? And that’s why I’ll always be indebted to him, man. I was on tour with Brook…

114.t: Learning chords from Tom MacIntosh; musicians who would not share
114.s: He first learned from Dizzy's quintet; Tom MacIntosh showed him chords on tour, and early colleagues guarded their licks.
114.ch: Alcohol, Paris and the hit record
114.q: Oh, no. I didn't find all that out until I got with Dizzy's quintet. And then when I got with Dizzy's quintet, then Dizzy didn't practice per se, like other people did. He'd sit at the piano and do things then apply it to his horn. Okay? You see? Then I had my septet and I'm in Philadelphia at the…

114.t: Learning by ear; not knowing whom to ask
114.s: He learned by listening to records and wonders how people like Wayne Shorter found where to study.
114.q: -- and just keep listening and listening and it would get in my ear and I would try to do it on my own, something like that.

114.t: No jam sessions; older players didn't know scales
114.s: When he came up there were few jam sessions or books, and he thinks older players knew little about scales.
114.q: No. We -- I didn't go to jam sessions because in the first place, don't forget, when I was coming up there weren't as many musicians as there are now, I don't think.

929.t: Starting a band by ear: simple blues, chords and parts
929.s: DeVore explains how to get beginners playing: take melody and chords off records, start with a blues and simple parts for piano, trombone, clarinet and cornet, and learn chords as Johnny Wiggs showed him.
929.q: Well, I don't know exactly what you want, but... Neither do we. If you're just interested in the band aspect as opposed against the individual aspect, there's a few simple little things that can be done to make it pretty fundamental. Now, I think, from my own experience anyway, you've got to have…

929.t: Discipline, starting from a model, and brass band influence
929.s: Modern players struggle with the discipline of the style; DeVore discusses the Pee Wee Irwin George Lewis imitation, choosing a model, Jelly Roll's band-style piano and brass band roots.
929.q: Yeah, absolutely. Couldn't go wrong. Keep more harmony? Yeah, this process speeds things up. And then, you see, for New Orleans things, and this is the hardest thing, the modern guys could play New Orleans jazz if they wanted to, but the hardest thing to do is to funnel all this background and…

612.t: Learning jazz from string bands and blues changes
612.s: He learned from visiting string musicians; jazz is attack on notes and adding passing chords to a twelve-bar blues.
612.q: No, well from other string band musicians coming through there and they’re playing different tunes and as far as jazz, I mean jazz is just the way you attack some notes, you know, from like an eighth note to a sixteenth note or something. And you go from just playing a tune with knowing the chords…

612.t: How guitar harmony helped his jazz violin
612.s: He explains learning violin with no frets, using chord knowledge, and that jazz was not taught in school.
612.q: Well on account of me knowing about the changes, chords and things, you know? And when I took my first lesson I could play better than the teacher but I didn’t know what I was playing so I still had to start over from, you know, C-D-E-F-G-A-D and down, and bowing all day and all of that. But it…

955.t: Learning to read and piano influences
955.s: He learned to read on jitney jobs, was taught chords by David John, and admired house-party pianists like Lil Willie.
955.q: No I wasn't. I learned how to read after I went to play on a Jitney job. Oh I see. I used to buy so much music I just had to learn something. I had fellows in the band to help me and sing along until I learned as much as I did now.

293.s: No piano teacher; he picked it up from banjo and guitar and got some chord lessons from Johnny Sincere, not learning to read.
293.q: I got a guitar, I got an amplifier, I got a recording outfit and everything right in there.

741.t: Learning chords by rote, and Wes Montgomery at Berklee
741.s: He learned chord melodies by ear before knowing names; Wes Montgomery soloed by ear at a Berklee workshop.
741.q: Yeah, sometimes. Sometimes we would do that. I didn’t really know the names of everything I was playing. Yeah I would just kind of give them one of these you know, and then other guys would go wow, look at that, I mean he can stretch more than one fret, how can he do that? And then later I started…

652.t: Roger Pemberton, the C sharp 7 sharp 9 chord and learning to hear intervals
652.s: At IU, Pemberton named a Horace Silver chord by ear; Buddy Baker's pitch pipe advice and realizing Oscar Peterson was not born special.
652.q: That’s my phone but I’m going to let it ring. That chord I found in school when I was in college and that’s a C sharp 7 sharp 9 and that’s something that Horace Silver played.

458.t: Self-taught players and fixed Do solfeggio
458.s: Beal discusses Erroll Garner and Eddie Diehl, reading being overrated, Mingus rehearsing without music, and a Jean Morel solfeggio story at Juilliard.
458.q: Well the first one I learned from was Erroll Garner on his records. He was self-taught. He couldn’t read music. And years later Woody Herman made a record, a duet record with him and we were playing at Basin Street and they were promoting that record and they invited Erroll to come and play with…

393.t: Learning by ear, the Clarkston jam sessions and Tad Weed on chords
393.s: He learned from records, a teacher Jamie McLeod and old-timer jams at 13, only grasping chords in his twenties from Tad Weed; now he is brushing up on reading.
393.q: Chords came much later. But as far as knowing keys and form when I was 13 my dad saw an ad in the local paper and it said the Clarkston — Clarkston is a town right near where I live here. I live in Waterford, Michigan. And it said that the Clarkston Senior Center, they were having, every Tuesday, a…

940.t: Cush Griffith, learning the show by ear, and Bobby Womack
940.s: Trumpeter Richard 'Cush' Griffith's charts went unused as Buddy Miles sang the licks; Bobby Womack also disliked charts, and Rowe agrees on playing by ear.
940.q: Well it’s funny you should say that because when we were rehearsing, we were rehearsing to go into the recording studio then go on the road, so there was a record attached to this Buddy Miles thing. When we went into the studio, and this guy named Richard Griffin — Richard Griffith, and his, they…

1032.t: Learning by ear: Toronto matinees, visiting players and Cuban barrios
1032.s: She is not an academic; she learned from Colonial Tavern shows, lessons from visiting musicians, and by hanging out with Cuban folkloric players.
1032.q: Maybe, maybe some vocal — some of the vocal things when I got very interested in the Afro-Cuban folkloric music so I would transcribe maybe some of the vocal lines because of the melodies that were so lovely and some of the Afro-Cuban chants. But both musics, I am not an academic and I’ll be…

592.t: Self-taught bandmates and being seen as over-intellectual
592.s: Older bandmates learned by ear; Coker's thoughtful approach, inherited from his family, set him apart.
592.q: Oh yeah, right. No I think it’s been very recent that musicians learn to do what they learn now in a college or a university. It wasn’t like that, you know, at the time I was growing up. And it certainly wasn’t like that at the time the other players in the band were growing up, because they were…

518.t: Perfect pitch and learning changes playing blues with his brother
518.s: Born with perfect pitch, he learned chord changes at twelve by playing blues choruses with his brother and Lenny Russo.
518.q: Yes I do. I do. And I learned that — I was born with perfect pitch so I hear all the inner voices and everything that’s going on, I hear them all. So when I first started playing jazz I was, well I was probably twelve. And my brother was — my brother was also a piano

693.t: Self-taught: chord books and piano players as teachers
693.s: He never had a teacher; he learned chords from a book and from piano players, and wanted to play jazz from age twelve.
693.q: Yeah, I got a book. And it had the little dots and the boxes on it. And pretty soon I got to be, you know and then I would always hang out with piano players, because the piano players were the theoreticians in the band. They’d all, all the guys I mean who played the piano usually had three or four…

514.s: He took only a couple of conservatory lessons, learned chords from the band director and a fake book, and his ear opened up in Chicago's rich piano scene.
514.q: All self-taught. All self-taught. As a matter of fact I went to the Chicago Conservatory and I went down, and I took a couple of lessons, but what it was was a case where I was memorizing the music. You probably heard this before from different people. It was like I was memorizing the music quicker…

938.t: Learning jazz by doing it and from records
938.s: No schools taught jazz; they learned at sessions and by copying 78 rpm records, and Noto was on the road with Kenton while Menza was in the Army.
938.q: Absolutely. There were no schools. Academia still really hasn’t accepted jazz as a quote art form, and they really don’t know how to deal with teaching it. I mean there are so many, scores of different approaches to it. And some of them work, some of them don’t. I find the shortcoming — or…

732.s: Rowe and Pallo trade stories of players who found good chords without knowing their names, such as the San Francisco example.
732.q: Oh well see that’s what we were just talking about, great ears. It’s like this gentleman came up and played San Francisco [sings] I left my heart in San Francisco. He’d say — we’ll put it in C just make it easy — he would just go from C to G seven, instead of using the seven. It sounded pretty good…

1031.t: Real Books, and learning tunes by ear from Bucky and Joe Mooney
1031.s: He says he has songbooks rather than Real Books. He recalls Bucky teaching him chords by ear, a method Bucky saw in Joe Mooney's rehearsals.
1031.q: No. You know what they would find? They would find Cole Porter, I’ve got a whole thing over here, there’s Johnny Mercer, Sammy Cahn, Jerome Kern. We had the Real Book, the old school Real Book. Bucky had it in a binder. He used to — I think it was either me or him would say what you should do is…

575.t: Learning chords and form by ear, starting with Perdido
575.s: Smith recalls realizing there were chords in Perdido and showing the tenor player. They note that early jazz greats also played by ear.
575.q: That’s right. And the first tune that I realized there were chords in it that I kind of knew what they were was “Perdido” which is one of the things we would play in those days. And I remember talking to the tenor player and telling him, “Look at this” and showing him I could play a C minor and…

851.t: Danny Barker, Erroll Garner and music without schooling
851.s: Garner could not read music; Barker and Blue Lu Barker as examples of New Orleans musicianship unsullied by education.
851.ch: Early New Orleans experiences and sideman roles
851.q: Reeves and through just various associations, been very fortunate to have had the chance to play with some iconic musicians.

364.s: Learned from sheet music, then discovered chord symbols via books his father brought; began to see music as a living.
364.q: Sheet music. Originally sheet music and sheet music had the chord symbols and the melody and all that accompaniment and I played with the accompaniment and all, but I never knew what those figures were up above. Nobody ever told me. I had no theory. Never had theory in my life. And finally one day…

1042.t: Dyslexia, playing by ear and hearing bebop in everything
1042.s: Vega says dyslexia made chord theory hard but his ears were strong; Gary Bartz's remark, Dizzy's Things to Come, the Waverly Consort, and learning tunes by ear at Doc Russell's house.
1042.q: Okay so my thing is this. And I share this openly with my students and I let them know, don’t be scared. I am the poster child for dyslexia. So the whole idea of the note and how it matches up to a chord, that was a nightmare for me. I knew what the note sounded like, and I could hear the chords,…

133.t: Learning from George Shearing's simplified books; That Old Feeling
133.s: Outside formal study he bought simplified George Shearing arrangements, which gave him That Old Feeling, later his own version on Three Blind Mice with Blakey.
133.ch: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
133.q: Well, that would, uh, get, uh, uh, there were books, simplified books of George Shearing's arrangements, for instance, that I would buy. I would gobble these up and … 'cause they weren't that hard. They were purposely, uh, simplified and so I remember, uh, learning how

470.t: Learning from older musicians by imitation
470.s: Older players taught by imitation; Wes Montgomery told him he would hear it, and Slide Hampton wrote out positions.
470.ch: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
470.q: They helped in a way, by imitation. They did. Wes [Montgomery] didn’t read [music]. Consequently you would play, and he would tell you, “You’ll hear it.” You got it by imitation. To a certain degree, that’s probably one of the most revered traditions. With Slide and them, they were very gracious to…

565.s: Saavedra taught finger independence, which led to his left-hand tumbao with right-hand soloing on his first recording.
565.q: Claudio Saavedra. He was a Spaniard who then took me into another world, which was independence, truly independence of the fingers. I put my hands like that and I tell them 3-4, they go at attention at one turn, two turns. 2-4... It took me years, both hands. 1-3. 2-4. Then you get the independence…

408.t: LaRose's teaching: pop songs of the week and Benny Carter solos
408.s: LaRose teaches him by ear and chord, with the week's hit songs and transcribed Benny Carter solos and a Hodges feature by Ellington.
408.q: lesson without even trying. You know, I didn’t think it was any big deal, and if I had gotten a teacher, one of those straight-laced cats, you know, who would say “Hey, you know, How dare you? You’re playing by ear.” You know, this is our best friend [points to his ear] this guy right here,” and…

406.t: Learning chords, Frankie Trumbauer's style and starting to write
406.s: Hines bought him a Trumbauer record; he collected Trumbauer's recordings, copied his alto style, studied a banjo book for chords and began arranging.
406.ch: Chicago, Virginia Ravens and the northern territory bands
406.q: So he bought me a record of Frankie Trumbauer Trombaer singing the Blues." And I fell in love with that style so I started buying all the things that Frankie Trumbauer made, that he made

66.t: Jack Howard's influence on her left hand
66.s: Jack Howard taught her to play the left hand louder than the right and many professional things; he followed her mother's circle from Atlanta to Pittsburgh.
66.q: : Jack Howard was an influence as far as giving me strength on the piano. He told me always to play the left hand louder than the right because that's where the beat and the feeling was. It's just like a drum keeping a steady beat. He taught me a lot of professional things it would have taken me…

117.t: Lessons from the McPartland family: Dick teaches chords
117.s: Freeman took a few lessons from Jimmy McPartland's father, learned chords from Dick McPartland, and learned jazz from records more than clubs.
117.q: When I was -- I took a few lessons from Jimmy McPartland's father, who was a music teacher, and I didn't seem to like the lessons because that was -- I didn't like the discipline, you know, of sitting down and reading music at that time, and so I became bored with that and just went on my own way,…
